13360:
To reappraise something means to look at it again carefully and form a fresh judgment about it — especially after some time has passed, new information has come in, or circumstances have changed.

Think of it in two parts:

  • Appraise = to carefully study something and decide what you think of it — its value, quality, importance, or meaning.
  • Re- = to do that same thing again.

So to reappraise is to go back and ask yourself: "Now that I know what I know, do I still think the same thing about this?"
What Makes It Different From Just "Thinking Again"

This is important. Reappraising is not the same as casually reconsidering something for a moment. It carries a sense of:

  • Deliberate effort — you are consciously sitting down to evaluate something with fresh eyes.
  • A previous judgment already existing — you already had a view, and now you're re-examining it.
  • A meaningful reason to revisit — something prompted the re-evaluation: new evidence, a major life event, the passing of time, a failure, a success, or simply gaining maturity and wisdom.

The word carries a slightly formal, serious tone. It suggests that the act of looking again is thorough and meaningful, not just a passing second thought.

Example 1 — A person:
You once thought a colleague was lazy. But after working closely with them for a year, you discover they were dealing with a serious personal crisis. You now reappraise them — and realize they are actually resilient and dedicated.

Example 2 — A decision:
A government introduces a new tax policy. After seeing that it is hurting small businesses, officials reappraise the policy and decide to make changes.

Example 3 — Art or literature:
A film was considered a failure when it was released. Years later, critics watch it again with fresh perspective and reappraise it as ahead of its time.

Example 4 — A personal belief:
You grew up believing that success means earning a lot of money. After a difficult experience, you reappraise that belief and decide that success actually means having time for the people you love.

Example 5 — A relationship:
After an argument with a close friend, you sit quietly and reappraise the friendship — weighing the good years against the current conflict — and decide it's worth saving.

Almost anything that can be judged can be reappraised. Common things people reappraise include:

  • A person (their character, intentions, or ability)
  • A decision or policy
  • A belief or value
  • A relationship
  • A piece of work (art, writing, music, architecture)
  • A situation or crisis
  • Oneself (your own choices, behavior, or identity)

This is a subtle but important point. When you reappraise something, the conclusion is open. You might:

  • Change your view completely — you realize you were wrong before.
  • Partially revise your view — you refine and adjust what you thought.
  • Confirm your original view — you look again and decide you were right all along. (This still counts as reappraising — the process happened, even if the outcome stayed the same.)

The word doesn't promise a change. It promises a genuine re-examination.

Reappraise is a moderately formal word. You'll find it in:

  • News articles and journalism
  • Academic and professional writing
  • Thoughtful personal reflection
  • Political and policy discussions

In casual conversation, people might say "take another look at," "rethink," or "reconsider" instead. But reappraise carries a slightly more rigorous, considered weight than those alternatives.

• Reappraisal (noun) — the act of reappraising. "The reappraisal of his legacy took decades."
  • Appraise (verb) — the first-time version of the act, without the "re-."
  • Reconsider — similar, but lighter; to reconsider is to think again, while to reappraise is to evaluate again in a deeper, more structured sense.
  • Reassess — nearly identical in meaning; often interchangeable with reappraise. Both mean to evaluate again. Reassess feels slightly more analytical or systematic; reappraise slightly more qualitative and judgmental in the neutral sense.
  • Review — broader and more routine; a review can be a first look or a repeated one, while reappraise always implies going back.
The Single-Sentence Definition You Can Always Return To

To reappraise is to deliberately and carefully evaluate something again — a person, idea, work, decision, or belief — in light of new information, changed circumstances, or simply a wiser perspective, in order to arrive at a fresh and honest judgment.
13361:
To understand reappraised, you first need to understand its root word.

To appraise something means to carefully look at it, study it, and form a judgment about its value, quality, or importance. Think of it like giving something an official verdict after thinking it through.

Now, the prefix re- simply means again or anew.

So, to reappraise means to judge or evaluate something a second time — usually because something has changed: new information appeared, time passed, or the first judgment turned out to be incomplete or wrong.

Reappraised, in its adjective form, describes something that has already gone through this second evaluation. It is used to describe the subject — the thing, person, idea, or work — that was looked at again and given a fresh verdict.
Breaking It Down With a Simple Image

Imagine you're a judge at a fruit market. You look at a basket of apples and declare, "These are ordinary apples. Three stars." That's an appraisal.

A week later, someone tells you these apples are actually a rare variety grown only in one valley in the world. You study them again, taste them again, and now you declare, "These are extraordinary. Five stars."

Those apples are now reappraised apples — they are the same apples, but they carry a new, revised judgment after being looked at again.

When you call something reappraised, you are silently communicating several things at once:

  1. A first judgment existed. Something was already evaluated before.
  2. That first judgment has been revisited. Someone looked at it again, more carefully or with fresh eyes.
  3. A new, often different conclusion has been reached. The outcome of this second look may confirm, upgrade, downgrade, or completely overturn the original verdict.
  4. The subject is now seen in a new light. The reappraised thing stands in a different position in people's understanding or estimation.

This is an important point: reappraised does not simply mean "evaluated." It specifically signals that a change in perspective or judgment has occurred after a previous one. If there was no first appraisal, there can be no reappraisal.
Where You Will Encounter This Word

Reappraised is used across many areas of life. Here are the most common ones:

Art and Literature
A novel that was ignored when first published but is later recognized as a masterpiece is called a reappraised work. The book itself didn't change. What changed is how people understand and value it now compared to before.

"The reappraised novel is now considered one of the greatest of its century."

History and Historical Figures
People from the past are often reappraised as new documents are discovered or as society's values evolve. A leader once celebrated as a hero might, after historians dig deeper, be reappraised as a more complicated or even troubling figure — and vice versa.

"The reappraised general is now seen as both a military genius and a deeply flawed human being."

Property and Finance
A house, a piece of land, or a company can be reappraised when market conditions change or when new information (like structural damage or a nearby new development) changes its worth.

"The reappraised property sold for twice its original estimated value."

Scientific and Medical Ideas
A theory that was once accepted, then rejected, and then proven to be correct after all, can be described as reappraised.

"The reappraised findings from the 1970s study are now considered groundbreaking."

Personal Beliefs and Relationships
Even in everyday life, a person's character, a past decision, or a belief system can be reappraised. Someone you once thought was dishonest, but later understood was acting under pressure, is a reappraised person in your mind.

Reappraised is not a neutral word. It carries a quiet sense of correction, maturity, and open-mindedness. When something is described as reappraised, it signals that people were willing to set aside their first impressions and look again — which takes intellectual honesty.

It can also carry a sense of justice, especially when someone or something was unfairly dismissed the first time and is now being given the recognition it deserves.

Occasionally, it goes the other direction — something once praised is reappraised and found wanting. In that case, the word carries a note of disillusionment or revision downward.
How It Sits in a Sentence

As an adjective, reappraised always describes a noun — the thing that has been evaluated again:

  • "The reappraised manuscript revealed a far more complex author than anyone had suspected."
  • "After decades of neglect, the reappraised paintings are finally receiving the attention they deserve."
  • "The reappraised evidence changed the entire direction of the investigation."
  • "She was a reappraised figure in feminist scholarship — once sidelined, now central."
Synonyms That Help You Anchor the Meaning

If you ever need a simpler word in place of reappraised, these work similarly:

  • Re-evaluated — looked at again and judged anew
  • Reassessed — measured or examined again
  • Reconsidered — thought about again with fresh perspective
  • Revised — (in terms of judgment) changed after review
  • Rehabilitated — (specifically when someone's reputation improves after being reconsidered)

None of these are perfect replacements — each has its own shade — but they all share the central idea of a second, fresh look resulting in a new judgment.

If you had to define it in one sentence:

Reappraised describes something that has been examined and judged a second time — usually resulting in a new or updated understanding of its value, quality, or importance.

That's the word in full. It's a small word doing big work: it tells you that something has a history of being judged, that judgment has been revisited, and that the subject now stands in a new light because of it.
13362:
When you say something is reasoned, you mean it is based on careful, logical thinking — not on gut feeling, emotion, or guesswork. A reasoned idea, argument, or decision has been thought through deliberately and methodically, with evidence and logic supporting it.

Think of it this way: if you arrive at a conclusion by actually working through the problem step by step, weighing the evidence, and building a logical case — that conclusion is reasoned. If you just blurt out whatever feels right in the moment, it is not.

The word carries a few important qualities at once:

1. It was arrived at through a process, not an accident.
A reasoned argument didn't just appear. Someone thought it through, examined the facts, and built up to a conclusion in an organized way.

2. It is supported, not bare.
A reasoned view doesn't stand alone as a naked opinion. It comes with backing — logic, evidence, clear explanation, or sound argument. You can look at the reasoning and evaluate it.

3. It is deliberate, not impulsive.
A reasoned response is the opposite of a knee-jerk reaction. The person paused, thought, and then spoke or decided.

4. It implies quality, not just effort.
"Reasoned" has a positive connotation. It suggests that the thinking was done well — that the logic actually holds up. Simply rambling through disorganized thoughts would not usually be called "reasoned."
Common Expressions Where You'll See It

• A reasoned argument — an argument built logically, step by step, with supporting points
  • A reasoned decision — a decision made after carefully thinking through the options and their consequences
  • A reasoned explanation — an explanation that makes its logic clear and follows a coherent structure
  • A reasoned opinion — an opinion that is backed by thought and evidence, not just personal taste
  • A reasoned debate — a debate conducted with logic and evidence rather than emotion or personal attacks
  • A reasoned approach — a method of doing something that is thoughtful, systematic, and justified

Understanding what "reasoned" contrasts with will sharpen your understanding:

Opposite typeWhat it means
EmotionalDriven by feelings rather than logic
ImpulsiveDone without thinking first
ArbitraryBased on no real logic or principle
InstinctiveBased on gut feeling, not worked-out thought
IrrationalContradicts logic or evidence

In short: anything unreflective, gut-driven, or poorly supported is the opposite of "reasoned."
Real-Life Examples to Lock It In

Example 1:

"The judge gave a reasoned ruling that cited three legal precedents and explained why each applied to this case."

Here, the ruling wasn't just "guilty" or "not guilty" with no explanation. It was backed by clear, step-by-step legal logic.

Example 2:

"She gave a reasoned explanation for why the company should invest in renewable energy — she presented data on cost savings, environmental impact, and long-term risk."

Her explanation wasn't just a vague feeling that renewables are good. It was structured, supported, and logical.

Example 3:

"His reasoned response to the criticism showed he had genuinely thought about the issue rather than reacting defensively."

Instead of snapping back emotionally, he calmly laid out a logical reply — that is what made it "reasoned."

Example 4 (showing contrast):

"She rejected the proposal not with any reasoned argument, but purely out of personal dislike."

The absence of reasoning is the point here — she had no logic, only feeling.

These words are easy to confuse, so here is how they differ:

Reasoned vs. Rational:
"Rational" describes a quality — it means in accordance with reason or sensible. A person can be rational; a system can be rational. "Reasoned," by contrast, specifically emphasizes that the process of reasoning was carried out — that someone actually did the thinking work. A reasoned argument is one where you can see the reasoning laid out. A rational argument is one that makes logical sense.

Reasoned vs. Reasonable:
"Reasonable" means fair, sensible, and within the bounds of common sense — it is a softer, more everyday word. You might say a price is reasonable, or that a request is reasonable. "Reasoned" is more specific and more rigorous — it means built on explicit reasoning and argument, not just sensible in a general way.

Reasoned vs. Logical:
"Logical" means following correctly from premises — it is about the structure of the argument. "Reasoned" includes that, but implies something more: a fuller, deliberate effort to work through a problem, present a case, and support a conclusion. All reasoned arguments are logical, but not everything called logical necessarily represents a full, deliberate reasoning process.
"Reasoned" means carefully thought through, logically supported, and deliberately argued — the opposite of emotional, impulsive, or arbitrary.
13363:
To reassure someone means to say or do something that removes their worry, fear, or doubt, and makes them feel calm, safe, or confident again.

Think of it this way: someone is feeling unsettled inside — nervous, scared, or uncertain. You step in and do or say something that settles them back down. That act of settling them is reassuring them.
The "Before" State: Why Reassurance Is Needed

Reassurance is only needed when something has gone wrong in someone's mind — when they are experiencing one of these:

  • Fear — "What if something bad happens?"
  • Doubt — "I'm not sure this is okay."
  • Worry — "I keep thinking about what could go wrong."
  • Insecurity — "Maybe I'm not good enough."
  • Uncertainty — "I don't know what's going to happen."

Without this troubled state of mind, there is nothing to reassure. This is an important part of the word's meaning — it always implies that someone was unsettled before the reassurance happened.
What You Actually Do When You Reassure Someone

Reassuring someone is not one fixed action. You can reassure through many different means:

  • Words — Telling someone that things are fine, that they have nothing to fear, or that the outcome will be good. "Everything is going to be okay," a mother tells her child.
  • Information or facts — Giving someone evidence or explanation that removes their fear. A doctor shows a patient their test results and explains that the numbers are completely normal.
  • Your presence or manner — Simply being calm and steady can reassure someone. A flight attendant's relaxed smile during mild turbulence reassures nervous passengers without saying a word.
  • Actions — Doing something that proves things are safe. A mechanic takes a car for a test drive in front of the worried owner to show it is working perfectly.

The key is that whatever you do must reach the other person's inner fear or doubt and dissolve it (or at least reduce it).

This is important: not only people can reassure.

  • A person can reassure another person. "Her friend reassured her that she looked wonderful."
  • You can reassure yourself. "He kept reassuring himself that he had studied enough." (This is called reflexive use.)
  • A thing, event, or piece of information can reassure someone. "The strong safety test results reassured the engineers." Here, the results themselves — not a person — are doing the reassuring.
  • A tone, look, or gesture can reassure. "His calm voice reassured the crowd."

After being reassured, the person typically feels:

  • Calmer
  • More confident
  • Less afraid
  • Relieved
  • At ease
  • More certain

They still know the problem or the uncertainty exists — but they no longer feel threatened or overwhelmed by it. Their emotional weight is lifted.

These examples show the word used in a variety of ways, so you can see how naturally it fits different situations:

  1. The nurse reassured the frightened child that the injection would only hurt for a moment.
  2. My manager reassured me that my job was not at risk despite the company's losses.
  3. She kept reassuring herself that she had made the right decision.
  4. His confident handshake and steady gaze reassured the client immediately.
  5. The clear weather forecast reassured the farmers who had been worried about their harvest.
  6. No matter how many times they reassured him, he remained nervous before the exam.
  7. The pilot's calm announcement reassured the passengers during the storm.

1. Reassurance does not guarantee truth.
When you reassure someone, you are trying to remove their fear — but what you say may or may not be true. A parent might say, "Don't worry, you'll do great!" before a performance without actually knowing how it will go. The intent is to comfort. Whether it turns out to be accurate is a separate matter.

However, in serious, responsible contexts (medicine, law, safety), reassurance is expected to be honest and accurate — a doctor should only reassure a patient if the situation genuinely warrants it.

2. Reassurance can fail.
You can attempt to reassure someone and fail. "I tried to reassure her, but she was still terrified." The action of reassuring requires that the other person actually receives and accepts the comfort. If they don't, the reassurance didn't "land."

3. Repeated reassurance can be a sign of deep anxiety.
If someone constantly needs reassurance about the same thing again and again, it often signals that they are genuinely struggling with anxiety. Each reassurance gives them only temporary relief. This is a nuance the word carries in psychological contexts.

4. Reassuring can be sincere or hollow.
"He said the words to reassure her, but he didn't believe them himself." Reassurance can be offered genuinely or merely as a social act to soothe someone — even if the speaker has doubts.

These words are close in meaning but not interchangeable:

Comfort — More general. You comfort someone who is sad, grieving, or in pain. It doesn't necessarily target a specific fear or doubt. You can comfort someone who just lost a loved one — not to remove their grief, but to be with them in it. Reassuring is more targeted: it specifically aims to remove or reduce a doubt or fear.

Console — Used when someone has already experienced a loss or setback. You console someone after their team loses, after a relationship ends, after a disappointment. Reassuring usually happens before or during the feared event, trying to prevent the fear from growing.

Encourage — To encourage is to give someone motivation and confidence to take action. "Go on, you can do it!" Reassuring is about removing a fear that is already there. The two sometimes overlap, but encouraging is more forward-pushing while reassuring is more fear-dissolving.

Promise — A promise is a specific commitment about a future outcome. Reassuring doesn't require a promise. You can reassure someone through tone, facts, presence, or explanation — without committing to any outcome.

All of these come from the same root and you will encounter them often:

  • Reassure (verb) — the action: "Let me reassure you."
  • Reassured (past tense / adjective) — describes the state after: "She felt reassured after the conversation."
  • Reassuring (adjective / present participle) — describes something that gives reassurance: "He had a reassuring smile." / "He is reassuring the patient right now."
  • Reassurance (noun) — the act or feeling itself: "She needed reassurance that she was loved."
  • Reassuringly (adverb) — in a way that reassures: "He spoke reassuringly."
One-Line Summary to Anchor It All
To reassure is to say, show, or do something that calms another person's fear, doubt, or worry — making them feel safe, confident, or at ease again.
13364:
Rebarbative means so unpleasant, harsh, or off-putting that it repels you — it makes you want to back away, avoid it, or stop engaging with it altogether.

Think of it as a combination of "repulsive," "uninviting," and "prickly." Something rebarbative doesn't just fail to attract you — it actively pushes you away.

What makes this word interesting is its degree and texture. It goes beyond simply calling something unpleasant or ugly. Rebarbative suggests something that has a bristling, hostile, or forbidding quality — like a wall of thorns rather than just a locked door. The thing or person doesn't just leave you cold; it makes you recoil.

Think of a cactus. It doesn't just fail to invite you to touch it — it actively warns you off. That quality, applied to something's appearance, manner, or character, is what rebarbative captures.

This word is flexible. You can use it to describe:

1. A person or their personality
A rebarbative person is someone whose manner is so harsh, cold, or prickly that others find it deeply off-putting. They don't just lack warmth — they project an almost hostile unwelcomingness. You've likely met someone who made you instantly uncomfortable, not because they did anything terrible, but because their entire manner seemed to push everyone away. That's rebarbative.

Example: "His rebarbative personality kept even his colleagues at arm's length, despite his obvious intelligence."

2. Writing, art, or ideas
Rebarbative writing is writing that is so dense, harsh, jagged, or difficult that it repels the reader rather than drawing them in. It doesn't flow — it grates. This is a common use of the word in literary criticism.

Example: "The philosopher's prose was notoriously rebarbative — full of jargon and convoluted sentences that made even experts struggle."

3. A place or environment
A rebarbative landscape or setting is one that feels bleak, unwelcoming, and harsh — the kind of place that seems to say "you are not welcome here."

Example: "The factory's rebarbative exterior — all grey concrete and rusted metal — matched the misery of working inside it."

4. An experience or task
Something can be rebarbative if it is so tedious, draining, or unpleasant that engaging with it feels like a form of punishment.

Example: "She found the hours of legal paperwork utterly rebarbative."

It helps to compare rebarbative with words that seem close to it, because each one occupies a slightly different space:

  • Unpleasant — general, mild, everyday. A bad smell is unpleasant. Rebarbative is stronger and more specific.
  • Repulsive — implies a strong sense of disgust, often physical. Repulsive is visceral. Rebarbative is more intellectual and temperamental — it's about a quality that pushes you away, not just something that disgusts you.
  • Forbidding — suggests something that looks stern or threatening. A rebarbative thing can be forbidding, but it also carries a sense of harshness and unpleasantness beyond just looking severe.
  • Abrasive — describes something (often a personality) that irritates through friction. Abrasive is a common word; rebarbative is rarer and more literary, with a stronger sense of repulsion.
  • Off-putting — the most casual near-synonym. Rebarbative is the formal, elevated version of off-putting, and implies a greater degree of the quality.

So if "off-putting" is a yellow flag, rebarbative is a red one.

This is an elevated, literary word. You are very unlikely to hear it in casual conversation. It lives in book reviews, essays, literary criticism, and careful writing. Using it signals that you are precise with language and have a wide vocabulary. If you use it in everyday speech, it will sound deliberately formal — which can itself be a stylistic choice.

Its strength on the scale of negativity is high. It's not a gentle criticism. Calling something rebarbative is saying it has a hard, hostile unpleasantness about it that makes people want to disengage.

If you want a simple mental image to remember this word: picture a person with their arms crossed, jaw set, and eyes cold — radiating a "stay away from me" energy. They aren't shouting or being aggressive. They are simply radiating an aura so uninviting that everyone around them takes a step back. That quality — in a person, a piece of writing, a place, or an experience — is what rebarbative means.
13365:
A rebate is a sum of money that is given back to you after you have already paid for something. Think of it as a delayed, partial refund — but not because something went wrong. It is a planned, intentional return of a portion of the money you spent, usually offered as an incentive or reward.

The single most important thing to understand about a rebate is timing: the money comes back to you after the purchase, not at the moment of buying.

1. You pay the full price for something upfront.
  2. Later — sometimes days, sometimes months — a certain amount of that money is returned to you.
  3. The net result is that you effectively paid less than the original price.

Imagine a new laptop is priced at $1,000. The store says: "Buy this laptop today, and we'll send you a $150 rebate."

Here is what happens:

  • You pay $1,000 at checkout. The full amount. No discount at the register.
  • You then fill out a form (or submit a claim online), proving you made the purchase.
  • A few weeks later, you receive $150 back — either as a cheque, a bank transfer, or a prepaid card.
  • Your actual final cost was $850, but you had to spend $1,000 first and wait to get the $150 back.

That $150 returned to you is the rebate.
Rebate vs. Discount — A Critical Distinction

These two words are often confused, but they are meaningfully different.

A discount reduces the price before you pay. You walk up to the register, and the price is already lower. You pay less, right then and there.

A rebate is different. You pay the full price first. The reduction happens afterward, when money is returned to you.

Simple memory trick: A discount saves you money going in. A rebate gives you money coming back.
Rebate vs. Refund — Another Key Distinction

A refund is what you get when something goes wrong — a product is faulty, or you simply want to return it. You give the product back, and you get your money back (usually all of it).

A rebate is different in two ways:

  • You keep the product. You are not returning it.
  • It is planned and offered in advance as part of a deal or promotion — not a reaction to a problem.
Where You Encounter Rebates in Real Life

1. Consumer Electronics and Appliances
This is the most classic context. Manufacturers or retailers offer rebates on TVs, laptops, refrigerators, etc. to attract buyers without publicly lowering the sticker price.

2. Tax Rebates
Governments sometimes offer tax rebates — they return a portion of the taxes you have already paid. This can happen when you overpaid tax throughout the year, or when the government introduces a special policy to give citizens money back (e.g., an energy rebate to help with high electricity costs).

3. Insurance Rebates
An insurance company may return part of your premium to you — for example, if you drove very safely all year and the company had lower-than-expected costs.

4. Business and Trade Rebates
In the world of business, a supplier might offer a rebate to a buyer who purchases very large quantities. For example: "Buy more than 10,000 units from us this year, and we'll give you a 5% rebate on your total spending." This encourages loyalty and bulk purchasing.

5. Utility and Energy Rebates
Governments or energy companies often offer rebates to encourage eco-friendly behaviour — e.g., "Install solar panels and receive a $500 rebate." You pay for the panels first; the rebate comes later.
Why Do Sellers Offer Rebates Instead of Just Lowering the Price?

This is a smart question, and understanding the answer deepens your grasp of the word.

  • Not everyone claims them. Many people forget to submit the paperwork, miss the deadline, or find the process too tedious. The seller gets to advertise a low effective price, but in reality, a portion of buyers never collect the rebate. This saves the seller money.
  • It keeps the official price high. The listed price stays the same, which can protect a brand's image or satisfy pricing agreements with other retailers.
  • It collects customer data. When buyers submit a rebate claim, they provide their name, address, and purchase details — valuable information for the seller.
  • It delays the cash outflow. The seller keeps the full payment for weeks or months before returning any of it.
A rebate is a partial return of money to a buyer after a purchase has been made, given as a planned incentive rather than as a response to a problem.
A Note on the Word's Feel

In everyday use, "rebate" almost always carries a positive tone from the buyer's perspective — it is money coming back to you, which is a good thing. However, it is also a word that implies patience, because you must wait for that money, and sometimes effort, because you may need to actively claim it.
13366:
A rebel is a person who refuses to accept, obey, or submit to authority, rules, or an established system — and who actively pushes back against it in some way.

The key word here is actively. A rebel doesn't just quietly disagree. A rebel resists, challenges, defies, or fights back — sometimes loudly, sometimes through deliberate action, sometimes just by living differently and refusing to conform.
What Exactly Does a Rebel Oppose?

A rebel always opposes something in power — something that has authority or control over them. That "something" can take many forms:

A government or ruler. This is the most classic use of the word. Soldiers who turn against their own government and take up arms are called rebels. Historical independence fighters, people who overthrow oppressive regimes, groups that wage war against a ruling power — all of these are rebels in the political sense. The American colonists who fought against British rule were rebels. The French Resistance fighters who opposed Nazi occupation were rebels.

A social system or set of norms. A rebel doesn't have to carry a weapon. Someone who loudly rejects the values, expectations, and rules that their society, culture, or community pressures them to follow can also be a rebel. A woman in a deeply conservative society who insists on living independently, or a young person who refuses to follow the career path their family has laid out for them, can rightly be called a rebel in this sense.

An institution or organization. Within a company, a school, a religion, or any structured group, someone who openly challenges the rules, questions the leadership, and refuses to simply go along with how things are done is a rebel within that institution.

The common thread across all these cases: there is power on one side, and the rebel is the person on the other side who refuses to bow to it.
The Spectrum: From Mild to Extreme

Rebellion exists on a wide spectrum, and the word "rebel" covers the whole range.

On one end, you have a teenager who dyes their hair an unusual colour, wears unconventional clothes, listens to music their parents hate, and rejects the idea that they should live a "normal" life. They are a rebel in a mild, personal sense — they're pushing against social expectations.

In the middle, you might have a journalist who keeps publishing stories that challenge a powerful government, knowing they risk punishment. Or a scientist who publicly contradicts the accepted scientific consensus of their time because they believe the evidence points elsewhere.

On the far end, you have armed rebels — organised groups of fighters who take up weapons against a government or ruling power, willing to risk their lives to bring about change.

All of these people can be called rebels. The word stretches across this entire range.

Rebels are driven by many different things, and this is important to understand because it affects how we judge them:

Principle and belief. Many rebels act out of a deep conviction that the authority they oppose is wrong — morally wrong, unjust, or corrupt. They resist because they believe it is the right thing to do. Nelson Mandela fought against apartheid in South Africa because he believed racial segregation was unjust.

Personal freedom. Some rebels simply cannot tolerate being controlled, told what to think, how to live, or what to do. Their rebellion is driven by a deep need for personal autonomy.

Anger and injustice. A rebel might be someone who has personally suffered under a system and fights back because of genuine grievance.

Desire for power. Not all rebels are noble. Some people rebel against authority simply because they want that authority for themselves. A military general who leads a coup against a government isn't necessarily fighting for justice — he may simply want to rule.

This range of motivations is exactly why the word "rebel" carries no automatic judgment of good or bad.

This is one of the most important and interesting things about the word "rebel" — it is morally neutral on its own. Whether a rebel is seen as a hero or a villain depends entirely on your point of view.

The same rebel can be called a freedom fighter by one group and a terrorist or traitor by another, depending on whose side you are on. The people who rebelled against British colonial rule in India were called criminals and insurgents by the British government — and are celebrated as national heroes in India today.

In everyday life, a rebel student who questions a teacher's authority might be seen as disruptive and problematic by the school — and inspiring and courageous by their fellow students.

The word itself simply describes what the person does: they resist authority. Whether that is admirable or not is a separate question that depends on context.

That said, in modern popular culture, the word "rebel" has taken on a somewhat romantic and positive flavour. We tend to admire people who stand up against power, refuse to conform, and have the courage to be different. Think of how we celebrate rebel artists, rebel thinkers, and rebel leaders in history. This romantic image of the rebel — bold, independent, fearless — is very common in movies, music, and literature.
How a Rebel Differs from Similar Words

Revolutionary: A revolutionary is almost always a rebel, but not every rebel is a revolutionary. A revolutionary has a specific, organised vision for replacing the existing system with a new one. A rebel may simply want to resist or destroy the current system without necessarily having a clear plan for what comes after. Revolution implies a more complete and transformative goal.

Dissenter: A dissenter disagrees with an authority or mainstream view, usually through words and argument rather than action. A dissenter speaks out, objects, and protests. A rebel takes it further — they don't just disagree, they defy and act against the authority. All rebels are dissenters, but not all dissenters are rebels.

Outlaw: An outlaw breaks the law and operates outside of it. A rebel may or may not break the law — what defines them is their opposition to authority, not necessarily lawbreaking. A rebel might break laws deliberately as part of their resistance, or they might resist in ways that are entirely legal.

You will hear "rebel" used in both serious and lighthearted contexts.

In a serious context: "The rebel forces captured the capital city." / "She was a rebel who devoted her life to fighting for civil rights."

In a casual, lighthearted context: "He's always been a bit of a rebel — he refuses to wear a tie even at formal events." / "I stayed up past midnight eating ice cream straight from the tub. I'm such a rebel." (This last example is ironic and humorous — used to poke fun at a very mild, harmless act of "rebellion.")

This shows the word's flexibility. In serious contexts, it carries weight and gravity. In casual contexts, it can be used playfully to describe anyone who bends small rules or does things their own way.
The Single Most Important Thing to Remember

If you want to hold onto just one idea, hold onto this:

A rebel is someone who refuses to simply obey or accept what authority tells them — and does something about it.

The authority might be a government, a society, a religion, a school, a family, or any system of power. The "doing something about it" might be fighting, protesting, speaking out, or simply living defiantly differently. But the rebel's defining quality is that they do not quietly comply. They push back. And in doing so, they place themselves in opposition to whatever power stands above them.
13367:
To rebel means to actively resist, oppose, or fight against a power, authority, or set of rules that controls you — particularly when you believe that control is wrong, unfair, or simply something you refuse to accept. The moment you rebel, you are not just quietly disagreeing with something. You are pushing back against it with intention and action. You are, in effect, saying: "I refuse to follow this. I will not accept this authority over me."

The most important thing to understand about this verb is that you always rebel against something or someone. This is why the preposition "against" almost always follows it. You might say "The citizens rebelled against the government," "She rebelled against her parents' expectations," or "The soldiers rebelled against their commander." The target of the rebellion — the authority or system being resisted — always comes after "against."

What can you rebel against? Practically anything that exerts control or authority over you. The most dramatic examples are political: citizens rebelling against a corrupt government, colonies rebelling against an empire, or enslaved people rebelling against those who enslaved them. But rebelling happens at a much smaller and more personal scale too. A teenager who refuses to follow household rules, wears clothes their parents disapprove of, or openly defies family expectations is also rebelling. An artist who refuses to follow the conventions of their time, or a worker who refuses to follow unjust instructions from a boss — these are all acts of rebellion.

This brings out something important about the range and intensity the word covers. Rebelling can mean anything from a child refusing to eat their vegetables all the way to armed citizens overthrowing a government. When the scale is very large and especially when it involves violence or an organized uprising, we sometimes use stronger words like "revolt" or "revolution." But "rebel" comfortably covers this entire spectrum. The common thread is always the same: a controlling force meets active resistance.

Notice the word "active" here — it matters. Rebelling is not just quiet, internal disagreement. You can privately think a rule is unjust without rebelling. The moment you rebel, you are doing something about it. Your resistance becomes visible. You are acting against the authority, not merely thinking against it.

There is also a strong emotional dimension to this word. To rebel suggests a feeling of being oppressed, restricted, or so deeply opposed to something that you can no longer simply comply. It implies courage, defiance, and a refusal to be controlled. This is why, in everyday speech, the word often carries a slightly admiring quality. We tend to picture the rebel as someone who has the courage to stand up against something powerful. Whether the rebellion is right or wrong is a separate question — the word itself does not judge. A tyrant's soldiers and a freedom fighter can both be described as "rebelling," depending on whose perspective you take. The word describes the action, not the morality of it.

Compared to similar words: "defy" usually describes a single, specific act of refusal ("she defied the order"), while "rebel" tends to suggest a sustained attitude or movement. "Resist" can be more passive — you can resist temptation without taking dramatic action — whereas rebelling always implies active opposition to authority. "Revolt" is very similar but is often used for larger or more violent uprisings. "Mutiny" is a specific kind of rebellion — soldiers or sailors rebelling against their own military commanders. "Protest" focuses on expressing disagreement, often publicly, but does not necessarily mean taking defiant action the way "rebel" does.

Grammatically, "rebel" is typically followed by "against": to rebel against something or someone. It works in all tenses — "they rebelled," "she is rebelling," "he has rebelled against every rule he has ever known." You can also use it to describe a general tendency, as in "she has always rebelled against convention."

One final, subtle thing worth understanding: when we say someone is rebelling, we are acknowledging that there is a real power structure they are pushing against — an authority that genuinely has control over them, or at least believes it does. This is what separates rebelling from simply doing whatever you want. A completely free person choosing their own path is not rebelling. But a person under the thumb of an authority who actively pushes back against it — that is rebellion. The power imbalance is baked into the very meaning of the word.
13368:
Rebellious describes someone (or something) that refuses to accept authority, control, or rules — and actively pushes back against them.

The "authority" here could be a government, a parent, a boss, a school, a religion, a society, or any system of rules. A rebellious person doesn't just quietly disagree — they resist, defy, or fight back, either in words, actions, or attitude.

Rebellious has two layers:

  1. Rejection — "I don't accept this rule / authority / system."
  2. Resistance — "And I'm going to show it."

Without both layers, the word doesn't quite fit. A person who merely dislikes authority but obeys quietly is not rebellious. A rebellious person makes their defiance visible in some way.

People are the most common subject:

  • A teenager who stays out late, dyes their hair, and ignores every rule at home is rebellious.
  • A soldier who refuses to follow orders from a commander is rebellious.
  • A citizen who protests and fights against an unjust government is rebellious.

Behaviour or actions can also be rebellious:

  • Wearing banned clothing in school as a form of protest is a rebellious act.
  • Publishing forbidden books under a dictatorship is a rebellious act.

Attitudes and personalities can be described this way:

  • "She has a rebellious spirit" — meaning her natural tendency is to question and resist authority.
  • "He has a rebellious nature" — he instinctively pushes against rules and control.

Groups can be rebellious too:

  • A rebellious faction within a political party that refuses to follow the party's leadership.
The Spectrum: How Rebellious Can Look Different

Rebelliousness exists on a wide scale. It doesn't always mean dramatic revolution or open warfare. It can be:

  • Mild and personal — A child who refuses to eat what their parents put on the table and insists on cooking their own food.
  • Social and cultural — A young person who rejects the dress, music, and values of their generation and does the opposite of what's "normal."
  • Political and serious — A group of people who openly resist and try to overthrow a government they see as oppressive.

What ties all these together is the same spirit: refusing to comply and pushing back.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

This is important — "rebellious" is not strictly negative or positive. It depends entirely on your point of view.

  • From the authority's perspective, a rebellious person is a problem — disobedient, disruptive, uncontrollable, dangerous.
  • From the rebel's perspective (or a sympathetic observer), being rebellious can feel brave, principled, free, and heroic — especially when the authority being resisted is corrupt or unjust.

Think about it: historical freedom fighters were called rebellious by those in power — and celebrated as heroes by those they fought for. The word itself stays neutral; the judgment comes from who is speaking.

This is why "rebellious" can carry admiration in some contexts ("She was a rebellious genius who changed music forever") and criticism in others ("His rebellious attitude got him expelled from three schools").
What Makes Someone "Rebellious" vs. Other Similar Words?

• Disobedient — simply not doing what you're told. A child who doesn't clean their room is disobedient, but not necessarily rebellious. Rebellious is stronger and more deliberate — it implies a deeper refusal rooted in attitude or principle, not just laziness or forgetfulness.
  • Stubborn — refusing to change your mind. Stubbornness is about persistence; rebelliousness is about resisting authority.
  • Independent — preferring to do things your own way. You can be independent without being rebellious. Rebellious specifically involves a push against something — there's friction, defiance, a target being resisted.
  • Revolutionary — wanting to completely overturn and replace a system. A revolutionary is often rebellious, but "rebellious" is the broader term. You can be rebellious in small, personal ways without wanting to start a revolution.

When people say someone has a rebellious streak or a rebellious nature, they mean it's baked into their personality. They question things automatically. They don't take rules at face value. They ask "why should I?" before they obey. They resist being told what to do, what to wear, what to think, or how to live.

This is different from someone who is rebellious situationally — only in a specific moment of injustice or frustration. A person with a rebellious nature tends to carry that quality consistently, in many areas of life.

• "The rebellious students refused to stand up when the principal walked in."
  • "Her rebellious attitude made her unpopular with teachers but admired by classmates."
  • "He had always been rebellious, questioning every rule his parents set."
  • "The rebellious artist painted murals on government walls despite repeated warnings."
  • "Even as a child, she had a rebellious spirit — she never simply accepted what she was told."
  • "The rebellious province declared independence from the central government."
  • "His rebellious phase in his twenties — the late nights, the protests, the unconventional choices — defined who he later became."

If you had to capture it in a single line:

Rebellious means actively resisting or defying authority, rules, or control — not out of mere laziness, but out of a spirit of opposition, whether personal, social, or political.
13369:
A rebuff is a rejection — but not just any ordinary rejection. It is a sharp, cold, and blunt refusal given to someone who has tried to reach out, connect, offer something, or get closer to you. What makes a rebuff different from a simple "no" is the manner in which it is delivered. It is dismissive. It is abrupt. It shuts the other person down — often leaving them feeling embarrassed, hurt, or discouraged.

A helpful way to hold onto this word: think of "buff" as in polishing something — making it welcome and smooth. A re*buff does the opposite. It pushes something away, roughens the interaction, and sends a clear signal: *not welcome here.
The Three Ingredients of a Rebuff

Every rebuff involves three things working together:

Someone makes an approach — they offer help, express interest, make a request, or try to be friendly. The other person turns that approach away — not kindly, but coldly and abruptly. And the person who was turned away is left stinging from the experience.

Remove any one of these elements and it's not quite a rebuff anymore. A gentle "no, thank you" is just a polite refusal. What makes a rebuff a rebuff is the coldness, the bluntness, and the sting it leaves behind.
Everyday Situations Where a Rebuff Happens

In personal life. Suppose you try to comfort a grieving friend, and they snap at you to leave them alone. That cold push-away is a rebuff. Or imagine someone working up the courage to tell a person they like them romantically, only to be met with silence and a look of disdain. That painful shut-down is a rebuff.

In professional life. A salesperson pitches their product to a company, and the executive cuts them off mid-sentence and walks out. That is a professional rebuff. An employee suggests a new idea in a meeting, and the manager dismisses it without even listening. That dismissal is a rebuff too.

In politics and diplomacy. A country reaches out to another to begin peace talks, and the other country publicly and coldly refuses. Journalists would almost certainly call that a diplomatic rebuff. A politician attempts to form an alliance with a rival party, only to be flatly turned down — that, too, is a rebuff.
What a Rebuff Feels Like (The Emotional Weight)

This is important, because a rebuff is not an emotionally neutral word. It carries a sting. The person who receives a rebuff almost always feels some combination of embarrassment, rejection, discouragement, or wounded pride. They put themselves out there — they took a risk — and they were shot down coldly.

This is why writers and speakers choose the word "rebuff" over a plain word like "refusal." "Refusal" is neutral. "Rebuff" tells you the rejection landed hard. It paints a fuller picture of what the experience felt like.
How Rebuff Is Used in Sentences

Notice how naturally it slots into different situations:

  • "She tried to apologize, but her gesture was met with a sharp rebuff."
  • "After yet another rebuff from publishers, he began to doubt his writing."
  • "The ambassador's peace overture suffered a humiliating rebuff."
  • "His attempts at friendship were greeted with constant rebuffs."
  • "She had grown used to rebuffs, but this one still hurt."

You'll notice rebuff is often paired with adjectives like sharp, cold, stinging, humiliating, or painful. These adjectives reinforce the idea of a rejection that doesn't just say no — it says no in a way that cuts.
How Rebuff Compares to Similar Words

Rejection is the closest word, but it is emotionally neutral. If a university doesn't accept your application, that's a rejection — it doesn't necessarily feel cold or personal. A rebuff is a rejection with teeth — delivered in a way that feels dismissive or unkind.

Snub is also similar. A snub is when someone deliberately ignores you or treats you as beneath their notice — like a celebrity walking past a fan without acknowledgment. A rebuff is more active: someone reaches out, and the other person actively and coldly turns them away. Both sting, but a snub is more about being ignored, while a rebuff is more about being pushed away.

Brush-off is an informal version of the same idea. "She gave him the brush-off" means the same thing as "she gave him a rebuff," but it's more casual and conversational. Rebuff is the more formal, literary choice.

Setback is completely different — it means an obstacle or a step backward in progress. Don't confuse them.

Rebuffs are not all equal. A mild rebuff is a firm but cold "no" that still feels unwelcoming. A sharp rebuff is blunt and possibly rude — it makes the other person feel foolish for even trying. A stinging or humiliating rebuff is one that publicly or deeply embarrasses the person who reached out.

The word rebuff, on its own, already implies some degree of coldness. But the adjective you pair it with tells you just how bad it was.

If you ever want to check whether "rebuff" is the right word, ask yourself: Did someone try to reach out, and were they turned away in a way that was cold, blunt, or dismissive — leaving them feeling pushed away or embarrassed? If yes, rebuff fits perfectly.
